title: SEPTICISION - Automated point-of-care precision diagnostics in the "golden first hour" of sepsis
summary:
Sepsis/bloodstream infection is a life-threatening diaease. It is triggered by a dysregulated response of the immune system after exposure to a pathogen. Rapid and effective therapy with antibiotics is crucial for the success of the treatment, if possible within the first hour. However, in order to initiate an effective therapy, essential results about the clinical picture would have to be available within an hour (diagnostics). These include the causative pathogen and the susceptibility of the pathogen towards antibiotics. However, the currently available methods take too long (24-72 hours, depending on the pathogen). Therefore, antibiotics that are effective against a large number of pathogens (broad-spectrum antibiotics) are usually the therapy of choice in the beginning. These often do not work optimally and promote the development of pathogens that are resistant to a large number of antibiotics. Furthermore, it is difficult and not always clear to differentiate sepsis/bloodstream infection from other diseases that are not caused by pathogens and do not require the administration of antibiotics. The concentration of measured inflammatory values from the blood (CRP, PCT and IL-6) can provide crucial diagnostic information for this differentiation.
In order to determine the pathogen, its susceptibility to antibiotics and the determination of the inflammation values within one hour and directly at the bedside, a new type of diagnostic device is being developed. For this research project, an additional blood sample and an additional swab from the front section of the nose will be taken from patients with suspected sepsis/bloodstream infection as part of the initial blood collection carried out for standard diagnostics. The patient then receives further standard diagnostics and therapy. If the diagnosis of sepsis/bloodstream infection is confirmed in the standard diagnostics, a second blood draw is offered 48-72 hours later. The patient samples for this study will be collected and subsequently examined with the new diagnostic device. These results should be compared with the results of the standard diagnostic procedures. We aim to show an agreement between the test results of the new method and the standard methods. The time difference between the availability of the results of  standard diagnostics and the new diagnostic device will be determined. Furthermore, we will examine in which patients an earlier availability of the results would have led to a change in the course of treatment. By means of an nasal swab, a correlation between the pathogens occurring in the patient's nose and the course of the disease/severity of the disease will be established. The reduction of pathogens under antibiotic therapy will be examined with the blood sample optionally taken during the course.

interventions.name: In patients with suspected bloodstream infection, a blood sample is taken at diagnosis and after 2-3 days and a nasal swab is taken. These are examined with a point-of-care device newly developed for this study and compared with standard diagnostic methods. All patients receive standard therapy. Par

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Hospitalized patients >= 18 years with initial suspicion of sepsis/bloodstream infection
Existing consent for the study participation of the patient or the caregiver
Exclusion criteria:
Age < 18 years
Pregnant women
Disabled people unable to consent
Lack of consent to participate in the study
